catalog_quote: Stress is not contrastive in Dhivehi, and is hard to determine. Intuitive judgments show that the Dhivehi stress rule is as follows: (11) a. Stress the heaviest syllable of the leftmost foot: /da'nī/ 'is going' b. If the leftmost foot has no heavy syllables, stress the initial syllable: /'divehi/, /'aharen/ 'I'. Thus, Dhivehi is a weight sensitive system very much like Sinhala (Letterman 1997: 236-247). Other heavy syllables in the word receive secondary stress (") if they are not adjacent to the primary stressed syllable ('): /'aha"ren/ 'I', /ma'tindā"bōṭu/ 'airplane'.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive, weight-sensitive stress at the left edge: within the word-initial (two-syllable) foot, stress the heavier syllable (so a light-heavy beginning gets second-syllable stress, e.g. da'nī); if neither of the first two syllables is heavy, stress the first syllable ('divehi, 'aharen). Default = initial. Gnanadesikan 2017:37 (snippets) restates it as 'heaviest syllable, ties to the leftmost, else first syllable' with three weight grades (light CV, heavy CVV/CVC, superheavy CVVC).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Other heavy syllables in the word carry secondary stress provided they are not adjacent to the primary-stressed syllable (/'aha"ren/, /ma'tindā"bōṭu/). Gnanadesikan 2017:38 adds that light syllables may take alternating secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Cain notes stress 'is hard to determine' (intuitive judgments). Gnanadesikan 2017:38 (snippet) mentions a set of words with exceptional second-syllable stress, linked to Fritz 2002:47 (words that would have second-syllable stress in e.g. their indefinite form).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated on citation forms; Cain 3.4 adds that in content questions the nuclear High tone docks on a stressed syllable (phrase-level use of word stress). Long vowels and closed syllables count as heavy.
new_statements.identity_note: Cain 2000 describes standard (Male') Dhivehi, with separate chapters on southern dialects (Addu, Huvadhu, Fua Mulaku); the stress statement in ch.3 is for the standard language = dhiv1236. Gnanadesikan 2017 likewise describes standard Male' Dhivehi.

sources.note: Sec. 3.3 'Metrical Stress' (p.30 = p.55): stress not contrastive and hard to determine; rule: stress the heaviest syllable of the leftmost foot (/da'nī/ 'is going'); if the leftmost foot has no heavy syllable, stress the initial syllable (/'divehi/, /'aharen/); weight-sensitive like Sinhala (Letterman 1997); other heavy syllables get secondary stress if not adjacent to the primary (/ma'tindā"bōṭu/ 'airplane'). Sec. 3.4: in content questions the nuclear H tone attaches to a stressed syllable.

tone.quote: Stress is not contrastive in Dhivehi, and is hard to determine. [...] 3.4 Intonation Patterns A detailed study of Dhivehi intonation has not yet been carried out. For this current study I have analyzed speech samples, and made preliminary observations about the pitch contours. Declarative sentences generally follow an even mid tone, and drop off to a low tone at the end of the sentence: [...] The basic pattern for content questions is Mid-High-Mid. [...] In Dhivehi content questions, the nuclear High tone attaches to a stressed syllable. A Mid follows after the High, and continues for the rest of the utterance, Tag questions tend to be mid tone throughout

tone.quote: 1.5. Word accent as a rule falls on one of the first two syllables in Dhivehi. [...] To sum up these observations, the basic rule of Maldivian word accentuation can be stated as follows: The first long syllable in a word is stressed. This comprises syllables that are closed by geminates or consonant clusters. 1.6. Sandhi phenomena do not play an important role in Dhivehi.
tone.locator: Vol. I, 'Phonology', sec. 1.5 'Word accent' begins at the foot of p.47 and the summary rule + sec. 1.6 are on p.48; Addu interrogative intonation ('special accentuation of the last syllable') sec. 3.15 / 3.15.1.1, pp.244-245 (index: 'word accent 47, 48, 245; interrogative intonation 245').
